lesson.title: The Spanish Inside Your English
lesson.subtitle: The Latinate inheritance, el/la, quiero, and lo as 'it' walking left

hook.title: You Already Speak a Vast Latin Language
hook.content: English absorbed thousands of Latin stems directly and through Norman French. Whenever you reach for formal English words like inquire, desire, or pastry, Spanish is standing right behind them. The pastry is el pastel. The coffee is el café. And 'I want' is quiero — born from the same Latin root as English 'inquire'. You already own thousands of Spanish roots without memorizing a single vocabulary list.

footnotes.title: Why 'yo' Is Optional in Spanish
footnotes.content: In English, 'want' could be I, you, we, or they — so you must say 'I want'. In Spanish, the -o ending of quiero belongs exclusively to 'I', so speakers drop yo unless they mean 'I (and nobody else) want'!

pattern.title: el, la — and the Pronoun Walks Left
pattern.content: The coffee is el café. The pastry is el pastel. And here is the core habit this course will anchor from your very first sentence: when you want to say 'it', Spanish places the object pronoun right before the conjugated verb. 'I want it' — where 'it' refers to the coffee — is lo quiero. Word for word: 'it I want'. And because the ending of quiero (-o) already announces 'I', you only add yo when you want extra emphasis!
pattern.linguist_note: el, la, and lo all derive from Latin demonstratives ille, illa, illum ('that one'). Spanish pointers became both articles and object pronouns.
pattern.trap_note: Your mind will want to say *quiero lo for 'I want it', copying English order. In Spanish, the pronoun walks left: lo quiero.

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: el pastel, el café, quiero, tú, un poco, lo
exercises.meaning: cake, pastry, coffee, I want, you (informal), a little, it (masculine)
exercises.explanation: pastel and café are direct cognates; quiero comes from querer (inquire); lo is the masculine/neuter 'it'.

exercises.prompt: quiero ('I want') shares its Latin root (quaerere 'to seek/ask') with an English word for asking questions. Which one?
exercises.meaning: to inquire is to ask for what you seek or want
exercises.explanation: Latin quaerere ('to seek, ask') gave Spanish querer ('to want, love') and English query, inquire, require.
Quiero (I want) + el pastel (the cake). Because -o on quiero already means 'I', yo is optional.

exercises.idea: you are telling a friend you want it — and 'it' refers to the coffee
cues: it referring to masculine coffee is lo
the pronoun walks left: it I want
idea_parts: order: it I want → Lo quiero
exercises.explanation: Lo quiero — the object pronoun sits directly before the conjugated verb: it I want.

diagnosis.slip: the pronoun stayed after the verb, English-style
diagnosis.cue: Spanish says it I want: the pronoun takes one step left. Lo quiero — never *quiero lo.

exercises.prompt: Which English word-for-word blueprint mirrors Spanish 'Lo quiero'?
exercises.meaning: I want it (literal Spanish blueprint: It I want)
exercises.explanation: Lo quiero is word-for-word 'It I want'. In Spanish, object pronouns walk one step left of conjugated verbs.

summary.outcome: Convert pastel and café from English, use quiero without needing yo, and place lo as 'it' before the verb.
summary.takeaway: English Latin roots are a Spanish treasury — and Spanish object pronouns walk one step left: it I want.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on El Puente ([101] Hidden Twins: Places & Colors): see how zero-shift cognates give you places and colors immediately.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — 'I want it, a little'?
twist.explanation: un poco sits at the end, just like English 'a little'.

foreshadow.line: One vital piece sits waiting: la, the feminine article, has no partner yet. Its moment arrives in Topic 2 — and it will carry thousands of words on its shoulders.

pastel.etymology_derivation: Late Latin pasta ('dough, paste') gives English 'pastry' and Spanish pastel. A cognate on the table.

café.etymology_derivation: Turkish kahve → Italian caffè → Spanish café. An international word shared across Europe.

querer.etymology_derivation: Latin quaerere ('to seek, ask for') evolved in Spanish to 'to want' and 'to love'. When you make an inquiry in English, you are asking what you want.

tú.etymology_derivation: Latin tū — the ancient Indo-European second person singular, preserved in Shakespeare's thou.

yo.etymology_derivation: Latin egō → eo → yo. English 'I' descends from Proto-Germanic *ik, born from the very same ancestral stem.

el.etymology_derivation: Latin demonstrative ille ('that one') trimmed down over centuries to el. Spanish pointers became articles.

la.etymology_derivation: Latin illa → la. It functions as both the feminine definite article ('the') and the direct object pronoun ('her / it').

lo.etymology_derivation: Latin illum → lo. Walks one step to the left of conjugated verbs: I it want.

un_poco.etymology_derivation: Latin paucus ('few, little') gives English 'paucity' and Spanish poco.

cion.name: The -CIÓN Passport
cion.phonetic_rule: English -tion /-(e)ʃən/ becomes Spanish -ción /-ˈθjon/. Always stressed on the ó, and 100% feminine (la).
cion.historical_linguistics: Descends from Latin third-declension abstract nouns in -tiō (accusative -tiōnem). English borrowed thousands via French; Spanish evolved -ción directly.
cion.philological_note: Because every single -ción noun is feminine, this family hands you grammatical gender for thousands of words without memorization.

dad.name: The -DAD Quality Bridge
dad.phonetic_rule: English abstract nouns in -ty correspond to Spanish -dad /-ˈdað/. 100% feminine (la).
dad.historical_linguistics: From Latin abstract quality nouns in -tās, accusative -tātem. Spanish lenited the intervocalic dental stop to -dad.
dad.philological_note: City (ciudad), reality (realidad), university (universidad). The ending guarantees feminine gender.

mente.name: The -MENTE Adverb Engine
mente.phonetic_rule: Feminine adjective + -mente /-ˈmente/ forms adverbs corresponding to English -ly.
mente.historical_linguistics: Originates from the Latin ablative phrase [adjective] mente ('with a ... mind'). Because mens is feminine in Latin, Spanish preserves the feminine adjective stem.
mente.philological_note: Notice how Spanish preserves the feminine form: exactamente (not exactomente). If the base adjective carries a tilde, it keeps it: fácilmente.

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).

ico.name: The -ICO Bridge
ico.phonetic_rule: English adjectives in -ic / -ical correspond to Spanish -ico /-iko/ (masculine) / -ica (feminine). Always carries a written accent on the antepenultimate syllable.
ico.historical_linguistics: Greek -ikos passed through Latin -icus. In Spanish, these are palabras esdrújulas and must be written with a tilde.
ico.philological_note: Mágico, público, básico, económico, romántico. The tilde tells your voice exactly where to jump.

al.name: The -AL Invariable Passport
al.phonetic_rule: English adjectives ending in -al match Spanish -al /-ˈal/ with identical spelling and gender-invariable singular form.
al.historical_linguistics: Latin adjectival suffix -ālis ('pertaining to'). Both languages kept the spelling; Spanish stresses the final syllable.
al.philological_note: El plan natural, la idea natural: no gender change in the singular.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.

ct_to_ch.name: Latin -CT- ➔ Spanish -CH-
ct_to_ch.phonetic_rule: Latin medial -ct- palatalized into Spanish -ch- /-tʃ-, while English kept the learned Latin -ct- form.
ct_to_ch.historical_linguistics: The velar stop /k/ vocalized into a palatal glide [j] which then fused with the dental /t/ into the affricate /tʃ/.
ct_to_ch.philological_note: Noctem ➔ noche (nocturnal); lactem ➔ leche (lactose); factum ➔ hecho (fact); octō ➔ ocho (octave).

pl_cl_fl_to_ll.name: Latin PL-/CL-/FL- ➔ Spanish LL-
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.phonetic_rule: Latin initial consonant clusters pl-, cl-, fl- palatalized into Spanish ll- /ʎ/ (or /ʝ/).
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.historical_linguistics: The initial stop or fricative conditioned progressive palatalization of the liquid /l/ in Western Iberian Vulgar Latin.
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.philological_note: Clāmāre ➔ llamar (claim/clamor); clāvis ➔ llave (clef/clavicle); pluvia ➔ lluvia (pluvial); plēnus ➔ lleno (plenty).
